newsitem.title: FRANCE: French foes trade last charges in final rallies.
newsitem.headline: French foes trade last charges in final rallies.

text.p: In their last campaign rallies, Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged voters on Thursday to put France back on its feet while Socialist challenger Lionel Jospin battled to defuse charges he could derail a single European currency.

On the penultimate day of campaigning before the first round of the May 25-June 1 poll, the centre-right premier appealed to voters to chase away defeatism and warned that any Socialist-Communist win would entail a "cacophony" on Europe.
"Yes, France, the time has come. Get back on your feet!" an upbeat Juppe exclaimed at a rally in the central city of Lyon.
"I urge you to reject defeatism and doubt. To help those who need us, we must chase away depressing thoughts and recover the morale of the conqueror," Juppe said.
In a final display of strength and unity, heavyweights of the fractious ruling coalition shared the platform with Juppe.

They included former interior minister Charles Pasqua, often an outspoken critic of Juppe within the Gaullist UDF, and Education Minister Francois Bayrou and Finance Minister Jean Arthuis of the junior coalition partner, the UDF.
But other possible Juppe successors -- parliamentary Speaker Philippe Seguin, former prime minister Edouard Balladur and former finance minister Alain Madelin -- stayed away.

Former defence minister Francois Leotard told the rally a Socialist-Communist win would mean cohabitation, or power-sharing with three different outlooks: President Jacques Chirac's, the Socialists' and the Communists'. He said the latter two had radically different ideas on Europe.
Juppe has said Jospin's conditions and spending would make it impossible for France to meet fiscal targets for a single currency and would cause crisis in the EU.
Socialist Jospin, campaigning in Toulouse in the southwest, reiterated backing for a single European currency on four conditions, including the inclusion of Spain and Italy from the start.

He also advocated a fresh taste of cohabitation, or power-sharing. "We have twice had cohabitation between a left-wing president and a right-wing prime minister (under late president Francois Mitterrand). We should try the opposite," he said.

Socialist Mitterrand shared power in 1986-88 and 1993-95 with conservative premiers. Chirac called the early elections, partly hoping to work in tandem with an ally for the last five years of his seven-year term.

Polls before last weekend's blackout suggested the centre-right would retain power. But the stock market closed 1.6 percent lower, with dealers citing rumours of secret polls showing the government's lead narrowing.
Jospin insisted that any other parties in a Socialist-led coalition would have to adopt his line on the euro.

Apart from the inclusion of Italy and Spain, Jospin wants a European "economic government" as a counterweight to the planned EU central bank, a pact of solidarity and growth to combat unemployment and measures to avoid over-valuation of the euro.

Communist party boss Robert Hue sought to play down public rifts with Jospin, whom he has accused of seeking hegemony over the left. "Jospin can cohabit with Robert Hue on Europe...The remaining obstacles can be overcome," he told Europe 1 radio.
